# Competitive Battle Cards: حصتي (Hissati) – LuggageShare peer-to-peer luggage space sharing platform

Use these when a prospect mentions a competitor or asks "how are you different?"

## Market Positioning
Hissati (حصتي) positions itself as a Saudi, Arabic-first, community-driven alternative to traditional courier and postal services. It connects travelers with spare luggage space to people who need to send items between cities, mainly on Gulf and MENA corridors such as Riyadh–Cairo, Jeddah–Dubai, Riyadh–Amman, Dammam–Bahrain and Riyadh–Istanbul. Its core pitch is twofold: senders get a more affordable and personal way to ship, and travelers can 'earn money from your trips' by monetizing empty luggage space at a self-set per-kg price. Hissati frames itself explicitly as an intermediary marketplace rather than a shipping company. It builds trust through verified Google sign-in, in-app secure chat, payments held by the platform until delivery is confirmed, two-way ratings, and a clear prohibited-items policy. The brand voice emphasizes trust, transparency and community, backed by a small Riyadh-based team. The website contains no explicit comparison pages or competitor mentions; the competitive framing is implicit ('instead of expensive shipping services').

## Our Unique Strengths
- Saudi-based and Arabic-first peer-to-peer luggage-sharing platform with an English toggle, localized for Gulf and MENA routes
- Dual value proposition: senders save on shipping while travelers earn from spare luggage space, with traveler-set per-kg pricing
- Payments run through the platform and are released to the carrier only after the sender confirms delivery (escrow-like protection)
- In-app secure chat that protects personal contact details and keeps a record of agreements, plus photo sharing of items
- Two-way ratings and reviews to build community trust
- Explicit prohibited-items policy, including a 10,000 SAR value cap on cash, jewelry and high-value goods
- Local support team aligned to the Saudi work week (Sun–Thu, KSA time) with a 24-hour ticket response commitment

## Common Alternatives (Non-Competitors)
What prospects do instead of buying a solution like ours:
- Asking friends, relatives or colleagues who are traveling to carry items informally
- Posting requests in WhatsApp groups, Facebook groups or Telegram channels for expat communities (e.g., Egyptian, Jordanian or Filipino communities in KSA)
- Using traditional couriers (Aramex, DHL, SMSA, FedEx, UPS) and paying premium rates
- Sending via Saudi Post or other national postal services and accepting slower delivery
- Waiting until the sender's own next trip to carry the items personally
- Buying the item at the destination instead of sending it (local e-commerce like Amazon, Noon or Talabat Mart in the destination country)
- Hiring informal 'cargo' or door-to-door freight consolidators popular with expat communities for bulk shipments home

## vs. Grabr

**How we win:** Hissati is Saudi-based, Arabic-first (with English toggle), and focused on Gulf/MENA routes such as Riyadh–Cairo, Jeddah–Dubai, Riyadh–Amman, Dammam–Bahrain and Riyadh–Istanbul. It handles sending existing items between people on a per-kg price set by the traveler. Grabr is built around buying products abroad and having travelers bring them back.

**Their weakness:** Grabr is a shopping-and-delivery model aimed at cross-border purchases, mainly from the US and Europe. It is not designed for personal parcel sending between cities. It has little local presence, Arabic support, or GCC-specific route density, and it depends on the traveler buying goods upfront, which adds friction and risk.

**Migration angle:** Users who just want to send a personal item, gift, or document to family in Cairo, Amman, or Dubai get a simpler flow on Hissati: browse a trip, request kg space, chat, and pay through the platform. There is no product purchasing step, and the experience is local and Arabic-native.

## vs. PiggyBee

**How we win:** Same peer-to-peer luggage-sharing concept, but localized for Saudi Arabia and the Gulf. Hissati offers Arabic UX, Saudi support hours (Sun–Thu, 9am–6pm KSA), payments held by the platform until delivery is confirmed, in-app secure chat, and a ratings system.

**Their weakness:** PiggyBee is Europe-centric with a small community and limited liquidity on MENA routes. It has no Arabic-first experience and little brand awareness in KSA, and its payment and escrow protections are less visible.

**Migration angle:** MENA users who tried PiggyBee and found few or no travelers on their routes can switch to a platform built around Saudi and regional corridors. Payment is held until delivery and there is a local Riyadh-based team.

## vs. Aramex

**How we win:** Lower cost: travelers set their own per-kg price on spare luggage capacity, often well below express courier rates on international routes like Riyadh–Cairo or Riyadh–Istanbul. Hissati also adds community trust features and gives travelers a way to earn.

**Their weakness:** Aramex's international express rates are high for individuals sending small personal items. Customs handling and fees add cost and delay, and the service is impersonal for one-off consumer shipments.

**Migration angle:** Individuals sending personal goods abroad (family gifts, documents, small items) can save significantly by using a traveler already flying that route, and can coordinate directly with the person carrying the item.

## vs. DHL Express

**How we win:** A fraction of the cost for small consumer shipments on popular Gulf and MENA routes. The process is community-driven: chat with the carrier, share photos, and rate each other. Travelers also earn from spare luggage space.

**Their weakness:** DHL Express is premium priced and geared toward business shipments, which makes it expensive for casual personal sends. Duties and customs paperwork can surprise consumers.

**Migration angle:** Price-sensitive senders who don't need guaranteed express timelines can trade some speed and certainty for large savings, using travelers flying the same route soon.

## vs. SMSA Express

**How we win:** SMSA is strong domestically, but Hissati covers cross-border routes popular with Saudi residents and expats (Cairo, Amman, Bahrain, Dubai, Istanbul) at flexible traveler-set prices. Hissati also allows same-trip, hand-carried delivery with direct coordination.

**Their weakness:** International shipping is costlier and slower relative to domestic. Customer service complaints about delays and tracking are common across Saudi courier services, and there is no personal relationship with whoever handles the item.

**Migration angle:** Expats and residents sending items home or to family abroad who find courier international rates too high, or who want a personal handoff, can switch to a traveler already heading there.

## vs. Saudi Post (SPL)

**How we win:** Hissati can be faster than standard postal international service when a traveler is flying soon, and it offers direct communication with the carrier, photo sharing, and peer ratings. It is a more personal, transparent experience.

**Their weakness:** International postal delivery can be slow and unpredictable, with limited real-time coordination. Customs processing at the destination can cause long delays.

**Migration angle:** Users frustrated with slow or unpredictable postal delivery to MENA destinations can use a traveler on a specific date to get the item to the recipient within days of the flight.
